en: So I did mention before that you can use Bun
for package and project management. So in
the same project as before, same code or
almost the same code, I added a package
here, the Sod package, which I'm using in
index.ts to basically verify that only valid
form actions are submitted.
Sod is a third-party library that has
nothing to do with Bun that can be used for
adding type safety at runtime and for
validating user input at runtime, for
example. Here I'm using Zod to define the
list of actions I wanna allow in that action
schema and I use that down here to parse the
submitted form action to make sure that it's
either increment or decrement and other
values would not be allowed.
Now, Zod was added as a dependency here to
this project and you can add dependencies to
a project using Bun as a package manager
instead of npm
by using bun add or bun install.
So you could add Svelte by running bun
install svelte. In that case, you really
just replace npm with Bun and it'll work.
Or you use the shorter bun add, which does
the same thing though. So that installs the
Svelte dependency. Now, unlike npm, at least
at the point of time where I'm recording
this, Bun is a bit more secure out of the
box because it, for example, prevents
packages you install from running lifecycle
scripts that may be attached to it, which
can protect against some attacks like supply
chain attacks or certain forms of supply
chain attacks.
Now, it's also important to point out though
that even if you're using the Bun runtime in
your project, you can of course still use
any package manager of your choice. You
don't have to use Bun. Bun is a great
package manager in my opinion, also because
it's pretty fast, but you could use npm or
pnpm or any other package manager and still
use Bun for the runtime. So you can still
run a file with bun run even if you use a
different package manager. That's important.
Now, when using Bun as a package manager,
you also got some additional features. For
example, you got bun why
to
ask why a certain package is in your
project. So if I ask for Svelte, for
example, with bun why,
I see that it's a direct dependency of my
project, which is correct because it's
directly listed here.
But in the npm ecosystem, which still gets
used by Bun if you use it as a package
manager, your dependencies can also have
their own dependencies.
So if I take a look at my node_modules
folder, which is where these dependencies
get installed, I, for example, see that I
seem to have the @undegi/types package in my
project.
And you might wonder where that's coming
from. So you can just ask
bun why
@undegi/types and you see, aha,
that is a dependency of the @node/types,
which are a dependency of the @bun/types.
The Bun types, due to that Node.js
compatibility which I mentioned, include the
Node types, and those in turn use the
Undici, the Undici types. And that is where
this package is coming from. So that's also
nice to have.
And then you also have the bun update
command to, for example, update your
packages that are installed,
or bun upgrade to update Bun itself.
And for bun update, you can also add
--latest to ensure that the latest versions
of your packages are installed. Installed
instead of just installing the next safe
version depending on how the package is
stored in package.json. Because when
installing packages, by default they get
added with this little circumflex here in
your package.json file, which means whenever
you update them with bun update, for
example, you install the next safe version,
the next minor or patch version
specifically, not the next major version.
The idea here is that typically packages
publish a new major version whenever
something big changes, potentially including
breaking changes.
And to be able to update and not break your
app, you often add packages like this in
your package.json file. And that is indeed
the default how they are added when
adding them with bun add or install.
And that circumflex simply means whenever
you update a package, it will ignore major
version updates and only update for minor
and patch versions. And you override that
behavior If you add --latest, in that case,
it will
rewrite that dependency in here and make
sure that it truly installs the latest
version right now, even if that could lead
to breaking changes. And that's a little
nice convenience if you know that you wanna
update to the very latest version.
